title: Take the tax out of the envelope
allegory: Weight decay is a flat wealth tax on every weight; Adam slips the tax bill into the same envelope as the pay claim, where each account's loudness discount shrinks it, so the loudest weights barely pay, while AdamW takes the tax straight from the account at one flat rate.
map: a flat wealth tax on every balance
weight decay: shrink each weight a little every step
the tax bill slipped into the pay-claim envelope
Adam: add λθ to the gradient, then divide by √v̂
loud accounts pay almost no tax
big-gradient parameters get the smallest effective decay
tax taken straight from the account
AdamW: θ ← θ - γλθ, outside the adaptive step
credit: Adam as momentum plus RMSprop is Andrew Ng's framing from the Deep Learning Specialization.

chapters.name: The dodged tax
chapters.note: weight_decay=0.01 ... so why is this weight still huge?

cap.1: Weight decay is meant to gently shrink every weight a little each step, so none grows huge. Inside Adam, the busiest weights quietly dodge it.
cap.2: You set weight_decay on Adam and expect every weight to shrink at one rate. Weights with big gradients barely shrink; quiet ones shrink hardest.
cap.3: Adam implements weight decay as L2: λθ is added to the gradient, then divided by √v̂ with everything else. Effective decay ends up inversely tied to gradient scale.

cap.1: Picture a tax on every account. Adam puts the tax bill in the same envelope as the pay claim, and each envelope is shrunk by how loud that account is.
cap.2: Adam divides each parameter's update by its recent gradient size. Put the decay inside the gradient and it gets divided too: busy weights pay almost no tax.
cap.3: L2 in Adam: the update is roughly (∇L + λθ)/√v̂ via the moments. Large v̂ makes the λθ share vanish; tiny v̂ amplifies it. The intended prior is inverted.

parts.note: flat tax, straight off the weight

cap.1: AdamW splits the two jobs. The tax comes straight off the weight at one flat rate. Only the learning step goes through the loudness divider.
cap.2: Adam is momentum plus RMSprop. AdamW keeps both and moves one term: the decay γλθ is subtracted directly, outside the adaptive step.
cap.3: AdamW: θ ← θ - γλθ, then the identical Adam step on the unmodified gradient. Loshchilov and Hutter (ICLR 2019): L2 and weight decay match only without per-parameter rescaling.

chapters.name: Busy versus quiet
chapters.title: Decay each weight really gets: Adam, then AdamW (illustrative)

cap.1: Same tax rate, three weights. Under Adam the busy one barely shrinks and the quiet one shrinks hard. Under AdamW all three shrink alike.
cap.2: Under Adam the decay a weight actually gets scales like 1/√v̂, so big-gradient weights are barely regularised. AdamW makes it uniform, which is what decay was meant to be.
cap.3: Schematic: Adam+L2 gives per-coordinate decay ∝ γλ/(√v̂ + ε); AdamW gives γλ for all. Bar heights are illustrative, not measured.

chapters.name: The default trap
chapters.verdict: Set weight_decay explicitly, and keep biases and norm weights out of it.

cap.1: A common surprise: you swap Adam for AdamW, change nothing else, and training gets worse. The two come with different default tax rates.
cap.2: PyTorch's Adam defaults to weight_decay=0, AdamW to 0.01, so the swap silently switches decay on, undamped. Set it explicitly; exclude biases and norm weights.
cap.3: Use parameter groups to decay only Linear and Conv weights, not biases or BatchNorm affine parameters, and re-tune the learning rate per optimiser rather than carrying it over.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Learning rate and decay: separate knobs
Decay the weights, not the biases

cap.1: Every transformer you train in this course uses AdamW. Knowing where the tax is collected tells you what the weight decay setting really does.
cap.2: Because decay is decoupled, a sweep can search learning rate and weight decay as separate axes instead of chasing one tangled optimum.
cap.3: Decay decides which weights stay large, which shapes the weights you later read as circuits or steer. Know which optimiser and decay produced the model you dissect.

coda.title: Toy model: how much of a weight 1000 steps of decay remove, by gradient size

caption.1: Left means a quiet weight, right means a busy one. Slide the decay up: under AdamW every weight loses the same share; under Adam the quiet ones lose far more.
caption.2: The Adam curve falls as the gradient size grows, because the decay is divided by it. AdamW's line is flat. Loss gradients are ignored here: this is pure decay.
caption.3: Adam+L2 removes 1 - (1 - γλ/√v̂)^1000; AdamW removes 1 - (1 - γλ)^1000. The crossing at √v̂ = 1 is an artefact of using one λ for both; the 1/√v̂ shape is the point.

where_else: Parameter groups, which keep decay off biases and normalisation weights
Hyperparameter sweeps, which can tune learning rate and weight decay as separate axes once they are decoupled
Every transformer training run in this course, where AdamW is the default optimiser
Any optimiser that rescales gradients per parameter: a penalty folded into the gradient gets rescaled too

hamming.what: Adam with the weight decay subtracted straight from the weights instead of being added to the gradient.
hamming.when: Whenever you train with an Adam-style optimiser and want regularisation, which in this course means every transformer.
hamming.why: Adam's per-parameter divider also divides any decay hidden in the gradient, so the busiest weights escape it; decoupling makes decay uniform and separately tunable.

object.title: The tax surface
object.subtitle: How hard each weight is really shrunk, by gradient size and decay setting, in Adam or AdamW.

knobs.label: Decay inside the gradient (1 = Adam, 0 = AdamW)

cap.1: Adam's tax surface. One edge is how big a weight's gradients are; the other is the decay you typed. Height is the shrink it actually gets.
cap.2: x: the weight's gradient size √v̂. y: the λ you set. Height: effective decay under Adam with L2.
cap.3: Height ∝ λ/√v̂: a hyperbola in gradient scale for every λ.

cap.1: From the side: quiet weights tower on the left and busy ones lie nearly flat on the right. Same setting, very different tax.
cap.2: The busiest weights, often the ones you most want to keep in check, get the least decay.
cap.3: For fixed λ the decay ratio between two weights equals the inverse ratio of their gradient RMS.

cap.1: Switch to AdamW and the surface becomes a plain ramp. The shrink depends only on the decay you typed, not on how busy a weight is.
cap.2: AdamW: height depends on λ alone. Every weight, busy or quiet, is decayed at the same rate.
cap.3: Decoupled decay: γλθ per step regardless of v̂. The surface is flat along the gradient-scale axis.

cap.1: Part-way back towards Adam, the ramp bends again. Any tax routed through the divider brings the unfairness back.
cap.2: The fix is all or nothing: any decay that passes through the adaptive divider gets rescaled.
cap.3: Only the component of the penalty applied outside the preconditioner stays uniform across coordinates.

predict.q: Under Adam with L2 weight decay, which weight is decayed least?

options.t: The one with the biggest gradients
The one with the smallest gradients

predict.why: The decay rides inside the gradient and is divided by √v̂, which is largest for the busiest weights.

predict.q: You swap t.optim.Adam for t.optim.AdamW and change nothing else. What changes?

options.t: Weight decay switches on at 0.01, undamped
Nothing, they are the same optimiser

predict.why: PyTorch's Adam defaults to weight_decay=0 and AdamW to 0.01, so the swap silently adds decay.

predict.q: In AdamW, where is the decay applied?

options.t: Straight to the weights, outside the adaptive step
Added to the gradient before the moments

predict.why: That one move is the whole difference between AdamW and Adam.

object.where: Anywhere an adaptive rescaling would swallow a penalty meant to be uniform: apply the penalty outside it.
